blocks.html: To a robot, a picture is not a scene. It is a big table of numbers.

An image is a grid of pixels, $w$ wide and $h$ tall. A grayscale pixel is one number, usually 0 (black) to 255 (white), one byte. A color pixel stores three: red, green and blue. So a color frame takes $w \times h \times 3$ bytes.

Knowing the size of an image tells you what a small computer can handle. A 640 × 480 color frame is 921,600 bytes; at 30 frames a second, that is about 28 MB every second. Robots shrink images, turn them gray, or look at only part of them to keep up.
Forgetting the three color channels, or mixing up bits and bytes (8 bits make 1 byte).

Camera setups (approximate U.S. prices, 2026)
  • \$0: your computer's webcam with free Python image libraries.
  • About \$25 to \$35: a Raspberry Pi camera module for a Raspberry Pi you already have.
  • About \$60 to \$90: a small smart-camera board that finds colors and tags itself and sends results to a microcontroller.
Load a photo in Python and print the three numbers of one pixel on a red apple and one on a leaf. Which number is biggest in each?

blocks.html: The simplest way to find a red ball: keep the pixels that look red and ignore the rest.
Thresholding tests every pixel and keeps those that pass, making a black-and-white mask. A simple redness test: keep pixels where $r - \dfrac{g + b}{2} > T$ for some threshold $T$.

blocks.name: rb-threshold
blocks.cap: Slide the threshold. Too low, and the background sneaks in; too high, and the ball disappears.

blocks.html: A pure red has a big red number and small green and blue. White is bright in all three, so plain "red > 150" would wrongly keep white. Subtracting the other channels asks how much more red there is, which is closer to what our eyes call red.
Setting one threshold in a bright room and being surprised when it fails in a dim one. Light changes all the numbers; many robots use color spaces such as HSV that separate color from brightness.

sources.name: Richard Szeliski, Computer Vision: Algorithms and Applications, 2nd ed. (Springer, 2022), free online edition

blocks.html: The mask shows where the ball is. Now steer toward it.

The target's center (centroid) is the average column of the pixels that passed. The steering error is that column minus the image's middle column, $w/2$. Feed it to a proportional controller: turn toward the target, harder when it is farther off center.

blocks.name: rb-threshold
blocks.cap: The cross marks the center of the kept pixels. The readout gives the steering error.

blocks.html: This is closed-loop control with a camera as the sensor. Each frame measures the error and the robot corrects; as it turns, the ball moves toward the middle and the error shrinks. It is how many FIRST robots line up with targets.

blocks.title: Steering error
blocks.q: Image 320 wide; kept pixels in columns 210, 214, 220, 224.
blocks.a: 57 pixels right of center: turn right.

blocks.html: Measuring the error from the left edge instead of from the center.

Put a camera on your mobile robot. Each frame: threshold for your ball's color, find the center, and set the wheel speeds from the steering error. Start with a small gain and raise it until the robot turns briskly without wobbling.
Safety. Chase a soft ball in an open room at low speed, with the power switch in reach. Keep the robot away from stairs.

blocks.html: A camera squashes the 3-D world onto a flat image. A simple model tells us exactly how, and lets a robot measure distance with one camera.

In the pinhole model, an object of height $H$ at distance $Z$ makes an image $h = \dfrac{f\,H}{Z}$ pixels tall, where $f$ is the focal length measured in pixels. Know the object's real size, and $Z = \dfrac{f\,H}{h}$.

blocks.name: rb-pinhole
blocks.cap: Move the object closer or farther, or make it bigger. The image size changes as $f H / Z$.

blocks.html: Light from the top and bottom of the object passes through the pinhole and makes two similar triangles, one outside the camera and one inside. Similar triangles have equal ratios: $h/f = H/Z$. The Math Ladder's similar-triangles topic is all you need.

blocks.title: How far?
blocks.q: A 0.2 m ball looks 50 pixels wide, with $f = 600$.

blocks.html: Mixing units: the focal length is in pixels, and the size and distance must both be in meters (or both in centimeters).
Real lenses bend straight lines a little; camera calibration measures $f$ and that bending from photos of a checkerboard.
